profile.name: Grass dance
profile.tagline: A Northern Plains Native American dance characterized by rhythmic, symmetrical, sweeping movements and long, flowing fringe regalia.
profile.insight: A medicine man’s vision of swaying prairie grass allegedly restored a handicapped boy’s ability to walk, leading to the creation of the first grass dance.
profile.profile: The Grass dance is a dynamic, symmetrical style of Native American pow wow dancing originating from Northern Great Plains warrior societies. It is distinguished by the dancer's use of long, brightly colored fringe that mimics the movement of prairie grass, rather than the heavy feather bustles found in other styles. While now a staple of modern pow wow culture, the dance historically served as a sacred ceremony for healing and blessing the ground.
profile.profile_long: The Grass dance, also known as the Omaha dance, is a significant tradition originating within the warrior societies of the Northern Great Plains. Its origins are widely contested, with various sources attributing its inception to the Omaha, Pawnee, Anishnabe, Ponca, Dakota, or Ho-Chunk tribes. Historical accounts suggest the dance was not originally intended for entertainment but served as a sacred ceremony for healing and blessing the ground where a feast or special event was to take place. One foundational narrative describes a medicine man who instructed a handicapped boy to seek inspiration in the prairie; the boy observed the swaying of the grass and received a vision of himself dancing in that style, which resulted in the restoration of his ability to walk. Another tradition suggests that scouts would bless and flatten the grass for a ceremony or battle, tying braided grass into their belts, a practice believed to have evolved into the yarn and ribbon fringe seen today. According to Antoine Lonesinger of the Sweet Grass First Nation, the ritual was given to the Nehiyawak by the Sioux (likely the Dakota) from the bone grass spirits, specifically to aid a man in mourning who had become gravely ill. The dance is characterized by fast-paced, symmetrical movements. Dancers must ensure that whatever motion is performed on one side of the body is mirrored on the other to mimic the swaying of grass. A signature movement involves planting one foot firmly on the ground while the rest of the body moves around it, a gesture said to represent a warrior fighting even when staked down. The regalia is distinct from other pow wow styles, primarily because it lacks the heavy feather bustles common in other men's dances. Instead, it features brightly colored fringe made of yarn, broadcloth, or ribbon, which the dancer emphasizes through swaying. The dancer typically wears a roach headdress with one or two feathers or fluff antennae, along with an 'H-Harness' consisting of two long suspenders and a belt. Dancers may carry feather fans, mirror boards, scarves, dream catchers, hoops, or dance sticks. In historical practice, the dance was performed around a drum, with specific roles for drummers and drum keepers. A photograph from circa 1891 of a Grass Dance on the Beardy and Okemasis Cree First Nation illustrates the historical context, showing eighteen men, four of whom were drummers, with women seated in the background. Today, the Grass dance remains a living tradition, performed at modern pow wows across North America, though its historical roots as a healing ceremony remain central to its cultural identity.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in Northern Great Plains warrior societies. Stories include a vision of a handicapped boy observing prairie grass and scouts blessing ground for ceremonies. It was historically used for healing and blessing, not entertainment.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is fast-paced and symmetrical. Dancers tap or step on the drum beat. Movements include wide, sweeping motions to mimic grass and a 'staked' step where one foot remains planted while the body moves around it.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is centered on a drum. Historically, four drummers were required, with individual keepers for each 'leg' of the drum and a lead drum keeper.
sections.costume_and_setting: Regalia features long, brightly colored fringe of yarn, ribbon, or broadcloth. It includes a roach headdress, H-Harness, cuffs, and side tabs. It notably lacks the heavy feather bustles found in other styles.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically used for healing the sick and blessing the ground for events. It is now a prominent style in modern pow wow dancing.
sections.notable_figures: Antoine Lonesinger, Marvin Littlechild, Chief Beardy.
sections.lineage: Northern Plains warrior societies, including Omaha, Pawnee, Anishnabe, Ponca, Dakota, and Ho-Chunk traditions.

profile.sacred_note: Historically, the dance was a ritual for healing and blessing the ground, not for entertainment; practitioners should respect its origins and the protocols of the specific First Nations or tribes hosting the event.

teaching.level_notes: Intermediate: requires maintaining symmetry and fluid fringe movement.

music_profile.sound_description: The music is driven by a central drum played by multiple drummers, accompanied by group singing.

movement_profile.footwork: Tapping or stepping on the drum beat; one foot planted while the body moves around it.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Symmetrical movement to mimic waving grass.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Fast-paced, faster than Northern Tradition but slower than Fancy dance.

signature_moves.name: Staked warrior
signature_moves.description: One foot is firmly planted on the ground while the rest of the body moves around it.

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Lack of symmetry; failing to maintain the drum beat.

activation_questions.why_needed: The dance has sacred origins and is a living tradition; respectful engagement is required.

claims.text: The Grass dance originated in Northern Great Plains warrior societies.
claims.quote: The grass dance or Omaha dance is a style of modern Native American men's pow wow dancing originating in the warrior societies on the Northern Great Plains.

claims.text: The dance is characterized by symmetrical, sweeping motions.
claims.quote: The grass dance is a fast-paced dance consisting of sweeping motions and symmetry. Whatever the grass dancer does on one side of his body, he must also do that on the other side

claims.text: Historically, the dance was a healing ceremony.
claims.quote: The Grass Dance was a ceremony performed by Northern Plains peoples, sometimes for healing and sometimes to bless the ground where a feast or special event was to take place.

claims.text: The regalia features fringe rather than heavy feather bustles.
claims.quote: The main difference between grass dance regalia and the regalia of the other pow wow styles is that there are very few if any feathers compared to bustles of most men's dances.

claims.text: A medicine man's vision is one of the stories behind the dance's origin.
claims.quote: One is that a medicine man told a handicapped boy to seek inspiration in the prairie. There he observed the swaying of the grass and received a vision of himself dancing the same style as the grass.

claims.text: The dance involves a 'staked' step representing a warrior fighting.
claims.quote: One dance steps typical of this involves one foot being firmly planted on the ground while the rest of the body moves around it. This is said to show a warrior still fighting when one foot has been staked down.
